narrative:
The model estimates a 57% chance that you will leave your current job. Because this probability is above 50%, the company has decided not to offer you the promotion at this time.

The decision is driven mainly by three aspects of your profile. First, your overall work experience of 1–5 years was the strongest factor and pulled the prediction toward staying. Most employees the model expects to remain with the company also have relatively short total experience, so this actually worked in your favor. However, the two next most important factors pushed the prediction the other way. The fact that you have received other job offers while working here strongly signals higher risk of departure. Similarly, having spent 1–5 years in your current role—while common among those predicted to stay—still added some upward pressure once the model considered the full picture.

Taken together, the combination of external opportunities and your tenure at the company outweighed the protective effect of your limited overall experience, tipping the scales toward leaving.

You and the organization should consider two practical next steps. First, explore whether any internal changes—such as clearer promotion paths, better recognition, or improved work conditions—could reduce the appeal of outside offers. Second, it may be useful to have an open conversation about your career goals so the company can better understand how to support your retention.
